newsitem.title: UK: Major woos N Irish MPs with move to ease beef ban.
newsitem.headline: Major woos N Irish MPs with move to ease beef ban.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's government looked sure of surviving a key censure motion on Monday after it unveiled measures designed to win the support of a group of members of parliament from Northern Ireland.

Defeat on the motion, which criticises Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg for his handling of the crisis over mad cow disease, would trigger a vote of confidence that could force Major to hold a snap general election.

Shorn of an overall majority in parliament, the ruling Conservative Party is increasingly dependent for electoral survival on the nine members of the Ulster Unionist Party, which represents Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority.

The Ulster Unionists used their power in December to secure an increase in fishing quotas for Northern Ireland's fishermen and were pushing hard behind the scenes on Monday to win similar concessions for the province's beef farmers.

Defending himself against attacks by the main opposition Labour Party, Hogg told parliament he would soon submit proposals to the European Commission for a partial lifting of the European Union's worldwide ban on British beef exports.
The EU imposed the ban last March because of evidence that the invariably fatal mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans.
Consumer confidence in beef plummeted as a result of the scare, which has so far cost Britain 3.5 billion pounds ($5.7 billion).

But Hogg said he would probably be able to submit proposals within a couple of weeks for the ban to be lifted on herds that have been tracked from birth and have not been fed contaminated meat and bone meal, which is blamed for causing BSE.
Earlier, Irish Agriculture Minister Ivan Yates said in Brussels such an approach was likely to find favour in the EU.
"I detected a willingness amongst virtually all member states to pursue a regional... lifting of the ban," he said.

Although the "certified herd" scheme would be open to all British farmers, Hogg acknowledged it was "likely to be of particular benefit to the farmers of Northern Ireland" who he said had a powerful case to put forward.
Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind cut short an official visit to Hong Kong to be back for the late evening vote, and some sick members of parliament will be brought by ambulance to cast their vote.
But Labour's chief business manager, Donald Dewar, admitted the odds were stacked against his party.
"The government will survive in numerical terms because it looks as though the Ulster Unionists are going to stay out of the lobby," Dewar told Sky Television.
Hogg accused Labour, out of power since 1979, of mounting a cheap political stunt aimed at forcing an early election.

Major can delay the election until May, and Hogg dropped a clear hint that Major wants to soldier on until then in the hope of a revival in the Conservatives' fortunes -- a poll on Sunday showed them 18 percentage points behind Labour.

"They (Labour) recognise that the growing strength of the British economy and the increasing disagreements within their own ranks makes a Conservative victory in a May election extremely probable," Hogg said.
